title: The three steps
prompt: Which pipeline shape implements the classic watermark-based incremental copy from a source table?

options.text: Lookup the stored last watermark → Copy activity filtered to rows past that watermark → activity that writes the new watermark back.
options.why: Correct. Read boundary, copy the delta, commit the boundary — the documented three-step pattern.

options.text: Copy the entire table every run into a new table.
options.why: That is full copy; the watermark pattern exists to avoid it.

options.text: An eventstream with a Filter node on the date column.
options.why: That is streaming ingest, not the batch watermark pattern.

options.text: A KQL materialized view over the source.
options.why: Wrong engine family; the source is relational and the pattern is pipeline-based.

explanation: Lookup (read the boundary) → Copy (move what is new) → write-back (commit the boundary). Everything else in incremental design elaborates this skeleton.

title: Choosing the watermark column
prompt: Which source column makes the soundest watermark for incremental copy?

options.text: A monotonically increasing column that changes with every new/modified row — e.g., a reliable last-modified timestamp or an identity/sequence value.
options.why: Correct. The watermark must advance with every change the pipeline must catch.

options.text: A customer's first-name column.
options.why: Non-monotonic, changes without meaning, and repeats — useless as a boundary.

options.text: A randomly generated GUID generated once at insert.
options.why: GUIDs do not order; a higher GUID says nothing about recency.

options.text: The table's clustered index key, whatever it is.
options.why: Only if it is actually monotonic with respect to change time — the property matters, not the name.

explanation: A watermark is only as good as its monotonicity: it must strictly advance as data changes, so no change is ever skipped.

title: Updates to old rows
prompt: A source row from 2019 is updated today, but the watermark pattern copies only rows newer than the last watermark. What is the consequence and the standard remedy?

options.text: Timestamp watermarks miss updates to old rows; the remedy is change tracking/CDC at the source, or accepting the limitation deliberately (insert-only semantics).
options.why: Correct. Timestamp watermarking sees inserts/monotonic changes — true updates to old rows need change capture or an explicit design decision.

options.text: The pattern catches updates automatically because the watermark rewinds.
options.why: Watermarks only advance; rewinding them is a redesign, not the pattern.

options.text: The destination automatically detects and patches the changed row.
options.why: Nothing in a copy pipeline detects changes that were never copied.

options.text: Mirroring fixes it without any configuration.
options.why: Mirroring is a different feature for supported sources — not a property of the watermark pipeline.

explanation: This is the honest boundary of watermark incremental copy: it is insert/recent-aware, not update-aware, unless the source provides change capture.

title: The boundary overlap
prompt: A run copies rows with modified_at > lastWatermark AND <= runStart. Why is the upper bound important?

options.text: Without an upper bound, rows inserted during the copy itself can be caught twice across runs (or leak into an inconsistent snapshot); the bounded window keeps each run's result deterministic.
options.why: Correct. Bounding the window makes each run's copied set well-defined and idempotent-ish, instead of racing with the source.

options.text: The upper bound encrypts the copied rows.
options.why: Boundaries filter; they do not encrypt.

options.text: It is cosmetic — unbounded copies are identical.
options.why: Unbounded windows race with concurrent writes; the results differ.

options.text: The upper bound is required by the destination's schema.
options.why: Destinations do not impose watermark bounds.

explanation: Bounded windows (lower = last watermark, upper = run start) make each run a deterministic slice — the documented tutorial's shape.

title: Reading one value
prompt: Which activity reads the stored last watermark (a single value from a control table or query result) into the pipeline?

options.text: The Lookup activity, which fetches a query result (first row) into the pipeline for use in expressions.
options.why: Correct. Lookup is the documented activity for reading values into pipeline context.

options.text: The Copy activity, targeting the pipeline itself.
options.why: Copy moves data between stores; it does not inject values into pipeline expressions.

options.text: The Notebook activity.
options.why: It runs notebooks; the watermark read is a lightweight query, not a Spark job.

options.text: The Filter transformation in an eventstream.
options.why: Wrong engine family entirely.

explanation: Lookup fetches the boundary value into the pipeline; its output feeds the Copy activity's query via expressions.

title: Committing the new boundary
prompt: After a successful copy, the new watermark must be persisted. Which activities fit the write-back step? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A Script activity executing an UPDATE against the control table.
options.why: Correct — Script runs the boundary update.

options.text: A Stored procedure activity calling a write-back procedure.
options.why: Correct — procedures are a documented write-back path.

options.text: A second Copy activity writing the new boundary row to the control table.
options.why: Correct — a copy into the control table works as the write-back.

options.text: The pipeline's title being renamed to the new watermark.
options.why: Incorrect — renaming is not persistence.

explanation: Any activity that can execute a write against the control table fits; the requirement is that the boundary commit happens after (and only after) a successful copy.

title: When the copy fails mid-run
prompt: The Copy activity fails halfway through copying the day's window. What is the correct watermark behavior, and why?

options.text: The watermark must not advance — the pipeline's dependency (copy on success → write-back) leaves the old boundary, so the next run re-copies the whole window.
options.why: Correct. Advancing the boundary after a partial copy would skip rows permanently; re-copying a window is the safe, documented shape.

options.text: The watermark advances anyway; failed rows are re-copied by a separate magic process.
options.why: No such magic process exists; advancing loses rows.

options.text: The watermark rewinds by one day automatically.
options.why: Nothing rewinds automatically; the design simply does not advance on failure.

options.text: The pipeline deletes the destination table on failure.
options.why: Nothing deletes automatically; failures leave prior state intact.

explanation: The dependency design (write-back only on success) is what makes re-copying a window safe and complete — the failure semantics of the pattern.

title: Idempotent landings
prompt: Because failed runs re-copy their whole window, the destination write must tolerate re-landing the same rows. Which combination achieves that?

options.text: Write mode replace-per-window (staging then swap), or upsert/MERGE on natural keys, or append-to-a-raw-layer-with-dedup downstream.
options.why: Correct. All three are documented-pattern-compatible idempotency designs; the anti-pattern is blind append to a curated table.

options.text: Blind append to the curated table each run.
options.why: Re-landed windows would duplicate rows.

options.text: Manual deduplication by an analyst each morning.
options.why: Not an engineering answer.

options.text: Rely on the source to resend only new rows after failures.
options.why: The source knows nothing about the pipeline's failures.

explanation: Re-copyable windows demand idempotent writes: replace-per-window, MERGE upserts, or raw-layer-then-dedup. Blind append is the bug.

title: Managed incremental
prompt: The team wants incremental behavior without authoring the watermark plumbing. Which Data Factory feature offers managed incremental copy for supported sources?

options.text: Copy job, which provides built-in incremental copy for supported sources.
options.why: Correct. Copy job's documented incremental capability removes the hand-built plumbing.

options.text: A pipeline with 100 Copy activities.
options.why: More activities is more plumbing, not less.

options.text: A semantic model's incremental refresh.
options.why: That governs model partitions, not pipeline data movement.

options.text: An eventstream.
options.why: Streaming ingest, not batch incremental copy.

explanation: Copy job is the documented managed path: incremental behavior for supported sources without hand-authored watermarks.

title: Copy job or watermark pipeline
prompt: Which selection rationale between Copy job incremental and a hand-built watermark pipeline is accurate?

options.text: Copy job when the source/destination pair and transformation needs fit its managed capability; the hand-built pipeline when custom filtering, shaping or source constraints exceed it.
options.why: Correct. Managed-first, custom-when-exceeded — the documented decision shape.

options.text: Always hand-build: managed features are never production-grade.
options.why: Copy job is a documented production feature.

options.text: Always Copy job: custom pipelines are deprecated.
options.why: Pipelines remain the flexible tool; neither absolute is true.

options.text: The choice is purely aesthetic.
options.why: The choice is functional: capability fit.

explanation: Managed capability first; the watermark pipeline remains the escape hatch for shapes Copy job does not cover.

title: Mirror or incremental copy
prompt: For a supported Azure SQL Database where analysts need a near-real-time, as-is replica, which tool fits — and which need would flip the answer?

options.text: Mirroring fits the as-is near-real-time replica; the answer flips when the landing needs reshaping/filtering (pipeline/dataflow work), since mirroring replicates as-is.
options.why: Correct. As-is replica → mirroring; transformed landing → pipeline/dataflow tooling.

options.text: Incremental copy always; mirroring is deprecated.
options.why: Neither feature is deprecated; they serve different jobs.

options.text: Mirroring for reshaped landings; copy for replicas.
options.why: That reverses the two jobs.

options.text: The tools are interchangeable for every workload.
options.why: Replica versus reshaped landing is a real distinction.

explanation: As-is replication is mirroring's job; the moment the landing must differ from the source, pipeline/dataflow tooling takes over.

title: Model partitions versus pipeline windows
prompt: How does a semantic model's incremental refresh differ from pipeline incremental copy?

options.text: Model incremental refresh manages the model's own partitions (RangeStart/RangeEnd in Power Query); pipeline incremental copy moves data between stores. Different layers, different mechanisms.
options.why: Correct. One governs model partition loading; the other governs data movement — related ideas, different layers.

options.text: They are the same feature exposed twice.
options.why: They operate on different artifacts with different mechanisms.

options.text: Model refresh copies data into pipelines.
options.why: Models do not drive pipeline copies.

options.text: Pipeline copy refreshes semantic models directly.
options.why: Pipelines move data; model refresh is a separate operation.

explanation: Same idea (only-new-data), different layers: model partitions versus data-movement pipelines. Knowing which layer a problem lives in is the skill.

title: Parallel per-region copies
prompt: Twelve regional source tables must each be copied with their own watermarks. Which pipeline pattern scales this without twelve hand-wired copies?

options.text: A control (metadata) table listing regions and boundaries, a Lookup to fetch the list, and a ForEach with parallelism executing a parameterized inner copy per region.
options.why: Correct. The metadata-driven pattern plus ForEach parallelism is the documented scaling shape.

options.text: Twelve separate pipelines maintained by hand.
options.why: Hand-maintenance is what the metadata pattern replaces.

options.text: One Copy activity copying all regions unfiltered.
options.why: That loses the per-region watermarks and incremental behavior.

options.text: Twelve eventstreams.
options.why: Wrong engine family for batch copy.

explanation: Metadata-driven design: the control table is the configuration, ForEach is the loop, parallelism is the knob.

title: Setting the run's variables
prompt: Within a run, the pipeline must compute the current run's upper boundary (e.g., current UTC timestamp) and pass it to the Copy query. Which mechanisms fit? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Pipeline expressions with the built-in UTC-now function, evaluated in the Copy activity's query/source settings.
options.why: Correct — expressions evaluate dynamic values in activity settings.

options.text: A Set variable activity storing the computed boundary for downstream activities.
options.why: Correct — variables carry computed values across the run.

options.text: A Lookup against a source that returns its own current timestamp.
options.why: Correct — the source's clock can define the boundary, often preferable to the pipeline's clock.

options.text: A static date hard-coded at authoring time.
options.why: Incorrect — a static boundary makes every run copy nothing new after day one.

explanation: Expressions, variables, or source-side clocks — all documented ways to define the moving boundary; static dates defeat the design.

title: Filter folding to the source
prompt: For the watermark filter to actually reduce transferred data, where must it be applied?

options.text: In the Copy activity's source query — so the filter executes at the source and only the delta crosses the network.
options.why: Correct. Source-side filtering is what makes incremental copy incremental; post-copy filtering moves everything anyway.

options.text: In the destination's table after landing.
options.why: By then, all the data has already been transferred.

options.text: In the pipeline's retry policy.
options.why: Retries govern failures, not data selection.

options.text: In the monitoring hub's filters.
options.why: Monitoring filters observe runs; they do not shape copies.

explanation: Incremental copy is incremental at the source: the watermark predicate belongs in the source query, or nothing is saved.

title: Watching the runs
prompt: Operations needs failure alerts and run history for the nightly incremental pipeline. Which documented surfaces serve this? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Pipeline run history in the workspace/monitoring surfaces.
options.why: Correct — run history is the first-stop record.

options.text: Pipeline run failure alerts (documented alert configuration for pipeline runs).
options.why: Correct — documented alerting for run outcomes.

options.text: The Real-Time hub's stream catalog.
options.why: Incorrect — the hub catalogs streams, not pipeline runs.

options.text: The deployment pipeline's compare view.
options.why: Incorrect — compare diffs definitions, not runs.

explanation: Run history plus run-failure alerts are the documented operations surfaces; stream catalogs and definition compares are different features.

title: Two tables, one run
prompt: An order header and its line items must incrementally copy together, consistently. Which design concern is specific to this parent-child shape?

options.text: Each table needs its own watermark, and consistency between them (headers copied without their lines, or vice versa) must be handled by design — e.g., overlapping windows or a shared snapshot boundary.
options.why: Correct. Related tables drift independently; consistent parent-child incremental loads need a deliberate consistency strategy.

options.text: Parent-child tables cannot be copied incrementally at all.
options.why: They can; consistency is the design concern, not a blocker.

options.text: The destination enforces the watermark automatically.
options.why: Destinations store what they receive; consistency is the pipeline's job.

options.text: Only the child table needs a watermark.
options.why: Both sides move independently; both need boundaries.

explanation: Parent-child incremental copy is a consistency design problem: per-table watermarks plus an overlap or snapshot strategy to keep referential pairs together.

title: The initial load
prompt: The watermark control table starts empty. What should the first run do?

options.text: Treat the empty boundary as 'copy everything up to the run start', landing the initial full load, then commit the boundary — the pattern's own first case.
options.why: Correct. Empty boundary = full initial load within the bounded window; the pattern handles its own bootstrap.

options.text: Fail deliberately until someone inserts a date by hand.
options.why: That is an unnecessary manual step if the pattern handles it.

options.text: Skip copying forever.
options.why: Nothing would ever land.

options.text: Copy only rows from today regardless of history.
options.why: That silently loses the initial history.

explanation: The empty watermark is the pattern's bootstrap case: full initial load up to the run start, then continuous increments.

title: Copy job scope
prompt: Which statement about Copy job is accurate?

options.text: Copy job is a simplified, managed copy experience in Data Factory that can move data between supported sources and destinations, with incremental behavior for supported cases.
options.why: Correct. Copy job is the managed, simplified copy item — with incremental capability for supported pairs.

options.text: Copy job is a monitoring dashboard.
options.why: It is a copy item, not a dashboard.

options.text: Copy job only works with Excel files.
options.why: Its connector set is broad.

options.text: Copy job requires authoring M queries.
options.why: Copy job is the no-M-code, managed experience.

explanation: Copy job = managed, simplified copy (including incremental for supported cases) — distinct from pipelines and dataflows.

title: Late-arriving history
prompt: The source team occasionally backfills old data (inserting rows with old business dates but new modified_at). What does the timestamp watermark pattern do with them?

options.text: It copies them correctly on the next run — the watermark keys on modified_at, not the business date, so backfilled rows are 'new' rows to the pipeline.
options.why: Correct. The watermark follows the change timestamp; the business date's age is irrelevant to detection (though the destination's downstream logic should handle historical rows).

options.text: It misses them because their business date is old.
options.why: Detection keys on modified_at; backfills are caught.

options.text: It duplicates the entire table.
options.why: Only the new rows are copied.

options.text: It requires a full manual reload each time.
options.why: Not with a modified_at-based watermark.

explanation: Watermark on the change timestamp: backfills are ordinary new rows — the destination layer decides how to treat their historical business dates.

title: Dataflow incremental tutorial
prompt: For sources that need Power Query shaping AND incremental behavior, which documented pattern applies?

options.text: The Dataflow Gen2 + pipeline activity incremental pattern — the dataflow shapes, the pipeline drives incremental runs with a moving boundary.
options.why: Correct. That documented tutorial combines shaping with orchestrated incremental runs.

options.text: A semantic-model incremental refresh policy on the dataflow.
options.why: Model policies govern models, not dataflows.

options.text: Mirroring the source.
options.why: Mirroring replicates as-is; shaping requires the dataflow pattern.

options.text: A KQL materialized view.
options.why: Wrong engine family.

explanation: Shaping + incrementality = the documented dataflow-plus-pipeline pattern; the boundary moves per orchestrated run.

title: ForEach granularity
prompt: A ForEach loops over 50 partitions calling a Copy activity. What does the documented parallelism setting control?

options.text: How many iterations execute concurrently — trading run speed against source/destination load.
options.why: Correct. Parallelism is the concurrency knob: more parallel copies, more load on both ends.

options.text: The number of retry attempts per iteration.
options.why: Retries are a separate activity policy.

options.text: The order of iterations alphabetically.
options.why: Ordering is not what parallelism controls.

options.text: The destination table's compression.
options.why: Unrelated to the loop.

explanation: ForEach parallelism is the concurrency dial — tune it against what the source and destination can absorb.

title: Deletes are not rows
prompt: The source hard-deletes rows (DELETE statements). What does a timestamp-watermark incremental copy see, and what are the honest options?

options.text: It sees nothing — a hard delete leaves no row to timestamp, so the delete never propagates; the options are soft deletes, source CDC, or scheduled reconciliation against the source.
options.why: Correct. Hard deletes are invisible to row-level watermarks; every remedy changes how the delete is represented or captured.

options.text: It copies the deleted rows again to keep them current.
options.why: Deleted rows no longer exist at the source; there is nothing to copy.

options.text: The destination automatically deletes matching rows.
options.why: The destination only knows what the pipeline sent; deletes were never sent.

options.text: Deletes are propagated by the watermark advancing backwards.
options.why: Watermarks advance forward; nothing rewinds to re-scan history.

explanation: Hard deletes are the classic blind spot of timestamp watermarks: no row means no change signal. Soft deletes, CDC, or reconciliation are the honest designs.

title: Soft deletes as a pattern
prompt: The source switches to soft deletes (an is_deleted flag updated on the row). How does the watermark pattern handle that change?

options.text: The flag update advances modified_at, so the row is copied on the next run and the destination logic applies the flag — deletes become visible as data.
options.why: Correct. Soft deletes turn a delete into an update, which the watermark sees; downstream applies the flag.

options.text: The pipeline must be rewritten from scratch; watermarks cannot carry flags.
options.why: The flag is an ordinary column; the same watermark copies it.

options.text: The flag is ignored by the copy.
options.why: The copy moves all columns, including the flag.

options.text: Only DELETE statements can express deletes in a copy pattern.
options.why: Soft-delete rows are updates, which the pattern handles naturally.

explanation: Soft deletes convert deletes into updates: the watermark catches the modified row, and the destination applies the flag.

title: The stuck window
prompt: A control table's watermark is accidentally updated to a future date. What does the next run copy, and what is the remedy?

options.text: It copies nothing (no rows exist past a future boundary); the remedy is correcting the stored watermark to the last good value and re-running the affected window.
options.why: Correct. A future boundary filters everything out; fixing the stored boundary re-enables the window.

options.text: It copies everything since 1970.
options.why: A future boundary excludes, not includes.

options.text: The pipeline auto-corrects future dates.
options.why: Nothing auto-corrects stored control data.

options.text: The source must be restored from backup.
options.why: The source is fine; the control row is the problem.

explanation: Control-table hygiene is operational: a corrupted boundary filters everything out, and the remedy is correcting the stored value.

title: Governance for the control table
prompt: Who should be able to write to the watermark control table?

options.text: Only the pipeline's identity (and break-glass administrators) — analysts read it, but writes are the pipeline's job, since manual edits corrupt the incremental state.
options.why: Correct. The control table is pipeline state; least-privilege writes protect the boundary.

options.text: Everyone in the tenant with edit access.
options.why: That invites the corrupted-boundary problem.

options.text: Nobody, not even the pipeline — control tables are immutable.
options.why: The pattern requires the pipeline to update the boundary.

options.text: Only external partners.
options.why: No such requirement exists.

explanation: The control table is pipeline-owned state: least privilege for writes keeps the incremental story honest.

title: Dependency types
prompt: The watermark write-back must run only when the copy succeeds. Which dependency type expresses that?

options.text: On-success dependency from the Copy activity to the write-back activity.
options.why: Correct. On-success is the dependency type that gates the boundary commit on a clean copy.

options.text: On-failure dependency.
options.why: That fires when the copy fails — the opposite of the requirement.

options.text: On-completion dependency.
options.why: Completion fires on success AND failure — too loose for a boundary commit.

options.text: No dependency; both run concurrently.
options.why: Concurrency would commit boundaries for failed copies.

explanation: On-success is the load-bearing dependency of the pattern: it is what makes failure semantics safe.

title: The source without a change column
prompt: A legacy source table has no reliable timestamp or sequence column. Which options remain for incremental behavior? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Use source change tracking/CDC mechanisms where the platform offers them (and mirror or stream from them).
options.why: Correct — CDC-based features detect changes without a user watermark column.

options.text: Add a modified_at column (and maintain it) at the source, if the source team agrees.
options.why: Correct — the schema change that makes watermarking possible.

options.text: Fall back to scheduled full loads if neither is possible, sized to cost.
options.why: Correct — the honest fallback when no change signal exists.

options.text: Guess rows by row-count differences and copy the difference.
options.why: Incorrect — row counts cannot identify which rows changed.

explanation: No change signal means: create one (CDC or a maintained column) or accept full loads. Guessing is not incremental.

title: Sizing the window
prompt: Hourly runs copy small windows; a weekly backfill job copies a much larger window. Which operational note is soundest?

options.text: Window size drives run duration and source load — schedule/backfill accordingly (e.g., separate schedules or bounded backfill chunks) so a large window cannot starve the operational cadence.
options.why: Correct. Window size is load: chunk backfills and separate schedules keep the steady state healthy.

options.text: Window size has no operational effect.
options.why: It is the primary load lever.

options.text: All windows must be identical by design.
options.why: Different windows for different jobs are normal.

options.text: Backfills must be forbidden outright.
options.why: Backfills are legitimate when bounded and scheduled.

explanation: The window is the load unit: hourly drips and weekly floods need different schedules and chunking.

title: Timezone of the boundary
prompt: The watermark is stored as UTC; an analyst compares it to a local-time report and declares the pipeline 'a day behind'. What is the soundest response?

options.text: Normalize the comparison: the watermark and the data's timestamps must be compared in one timezone (UTC), and the report should convert for display only.
options.why: Correct. Mixed-timezone comparisons manufacture false lag; storage in UTC with display-time conversion is the fix.

options.text: Store watermarks in local time with DST.
options.why: DST transitions corrupt boundary arithmetic — UTC storage exists to avoid that.

options.text: The pipeline is actually a day behind and must be rerun.
options.why: The comparison was invalid; rerunning wastes a full window.

options.text: Timezones are irrelevant to watermarks.
options.why: They matter precisely because comparisons must be normalized.

explanation: UTC storage, display-time conversion — the standard boundary discipline that prevents phantom lag.

title: The parameterized copy query
prompt: In the tutorial pattern, how does the Copy activity's source query receive the watermark boundaries?

options.text: Through pipeline expressions/parameters interpolating the Lookup result and run boundary into the source query's WHERE clause.
options.why: Correct. The tutorial wires the boundaries into the source query via expressions — that is what makes the copy incremental.

options.text: The Copy activity reads the boundaries from the destination table automatically.
options.why: No automatic boundary reading exists.

options.text: Boundaries are typed into the activity each run by an operator.
options.why: That is manual operation, not orchestration.

options.text: The query cannot contain a WHERE clause.
options.why: The WHERE clause is the whole mechanism.

explanation: Expression-interpolated boundaries in the source WHERE clause — the tutorial's core wiring.

title: Three increments, three layers
prompt: Match the incremental mechanism to its layer: (1) model partitions; (2) pipeline/copy data movement; (3) managed database replication.

options.text: Semantic-model incremental refresh; watermark/Copy-job pipelines; mirroring.
options.why: Correct. Model layer, movement layer, replication layer — respectively.

options.text: Mirroring; semantic-model refresh; pipelines.
options.why: That mismatches every layer.

options.text: All three are pipeline features.
options.why: Model refresh and mirroring are different layers.

options.text: All three are semantic-model features.
options.why: Only the first is.

explanation: Incrementality exists at three layers for three reasons; matching mechanism to layer is the architectural skill.

title: Audit the boundary
prompt: For audit purposes, what should each run record about its window?

options.text: The exact boundaries used (old watermark, new watermark/run start), row counts, and run status — so any window can be replayed or investigated.
options.why: Correct. Replaying an audit requires the boundaries and the outcome; that is the runbook record.

options.text: Only the pipeline's display name.
options.why: Names carry no window information.

options.text: The source database's backup history.
options.why: Unrelated to the run's window.

options.text: Nothing — runs are ephemeral.
options.why: Auditability requires the record.

explanation: Boundary + count + status per run: the minimal audit record that makes windows replayable and incidents investigable.

title: Duplicate boundaries
prompt: Two pipelines accidentally share one control-table watermark row for the same source. What happens?

options.text: They race on the boundary — one run's commit skips the other's window, silently losing rows. Each source/destination pair needs its own boundary state.
options.why: Correct. Shared mutable state across pipelines corrupts boundaries; one boundary per pipeline/pair is the rule.

options.text: Nothing — boundaries are read-only to pipelines.
options.why: Pipelines write boundaries by design.

options.text: Fabric detects and blocks shared boundaries.
options.why: No such detection exists; it is a design discipline.

options.text: Both pipelines copy full tables every time.
options.why: They copy whatever the shared (racing) boundary says — which is the bug.

explanation: Boundary state is per-pipeline state: sharing it across independent pipelines is a silent data-loss design.

title: Lookup returned nothing
prompt: The Lookup activity that should return the watermark returns zero rows on the very first run. What is the soundest handling?

options.text: Branch on the Lookup outcome: empty result → use the defined default boundary (e.g., epoch or a chosen start date) for the initial load; non-empty → proceed normally.
options.why: Correct. The bootstrap case is a designed branch, not an error.

options.text: Let the pipeline fail every first run and rerun after inserting a row.
options.why: Failing as a design is unnecessary when the branch handles it.

options.text: Hard-code the watermark inside the Copy query.
options.why: That defeats the pattern's parameterization.

options.text: Delete the control table.
options.why: The control table is the state; deleting it loses the boundary permanently.

explanation: Bootstrap is a branch: empty boundary → default start → full initial load → commit. The pattern owns its first case.

title: Eventstream CDC or watermark copy
prompt: A SQL source supports both eventstream CDC ingestion and a watermark pipeline. The destination is a lakehouse table that must be a continuously current replica. Which fits better?

options.text: Mirroring-style continuous replication is the closer fit — but between the two offered tools, eventstream CDC lands changes continuously while a watermark pipeline lands on its schedule; pick by the required freshness and shape.
options.why: Correct. Freshness requirement decides: continuous change landing favors the CDC path; scheduled shaped landing favors the watermark pipeline.

options.text: The watermark pipeline is always fresher.
options.why: Scheduled copy is by definition batch-fresh.

options.text: Both produce identical freshness.
options.why: Continuous versus scheduled differ fundamentally.

options.text: Neither can land in a lakehouse.
options.why: Both can land lakehouse data through their destinations.

explanation: Freshness and shape decide: continuous as-is change landing → CDC path; scheduled shaped landing → watermark pipeline.

title: The staging swap
prompt: A window's copy lands into a staging table, and a following activity swaps/merges it into the curated table. What does this staging pattern buy?

options.text: Atomic-feeling cutover: consumers see the curated table only after the swap/merge completes.
options.why: Correct — consumers never observe half-loaded windows.

options.text: Easy re-runs: a failed window re-copies into staging without touching curated data.
options.why: Correct — staging isolates retries from consumers.

options.text: Automatic schema drift resolution with no design.
options.why: Incorrect — schema handling is still designed, staging does not solve it by magic.

options.text: Free compression of all data.
options.why: Incorrect — staging adds a copy step, not free compression.

explanation: Staging buys isolation: consumers see completed windows only, and retries never touch curated data. Schema drift and compression are separate concerns.

title: Testing the pipeline safely
prompt: How should the incremental pipeline be tested before pointing at production sources?

options.text: Test against a dev source/copy with inserted, updated, deleted and edge-case rows; verify windows, failure re-copies, and idempotent landings; then promote via deployment pipelines with stage parameters.
options.why: Correct. The test matrix mirrors the pattern's semantics: inserts, updates, deletes, boundary edges, failure replay, then staged promotion.

options.text: Run once against production and watch.
options.why: That tests on real data and real risk.

options.text: Trust the tutorial without testing.
options.why: Tutorials teach the pattern; testing validates the implementation.

options.text: Only test the success path.
options.why: Failure semantics are the pattern's core risk.

explanation: The test matrix is the pattern's semantics: boundary edges, update/delete behavior, failure replay, idempotency — then promotion.

title: Positioning in one line
prompt: Which one-liner best positions incremental copy for an architecture review?

options.text: Scheduled movement of only-new data between stores — watermark pipelines for full control, Copy job for managed capability — with failure semantics designed for re-copyable windows.
options.why: Correct. That line carries the two implementations and the load-bearing failure design.

options.text: Continuous managed replication of any database.
options.why: That is mirroring's line.

options.text: Streaming ingest of telemetry.
options.why: That is eventstream.

options.text: Model partition management.
options.why: That is semantic-model incremental refresh.

explanation: The one-liner test: scheduled, only-new, two implementations, re-copyable windows — anything else is a different feature.

title: The estate rollout
prompt: Ten source tables move to incremental copy. Which rollout practice is soundest?

options.text: One pipeline pattern (metadata-driven where possible), one control table with per-table boundaries owned by the pipelines, documented failure/idempotency semantics, and per-table run audit records.
options.why: Correct. One pattern, isolated boundaries, documented semantics, per-table audit — the scalable version of the recipe.

options.text: Ten pipelines sharing one watermark row.
options.why: Shared boundaries race and lose rows (see the duplicate-boundary case).

options.text: No control table; rely on memory between runs.
options.why: Pipelines are stateless between runs; state must be stored.

options.text: A different hand-built pattern per table.
options.why: Ten patterns are ten maintenance burdens; one pattern parameterized is the design.

explanation: Scale comes from one parameterized pattern with isolated per-table state — plus documented semantics and audit records.
